topic: Endowed progress effect, Nunes & Drèze car wash study

slides.title: A car wash gave away two free stamps.
slides.accent: Nearly twice as many people finished.

slides.body:
In 2004, marketing professors Joseph Nunes and Xavier Drèze ran an experiment with a car wash.

Customers got a loyalty card: buy eight washes, get one free. But not everyone got the same card.
Both needed eight more washes. One of them just looked 20% done.

Of the empty cards, 19% were completed.

Of the cards with two free stamps, 34%. And those customers finished sooner, too.

The free stamps changed only how the task looked: not “not started”, but “already underway”.

The researchers called it the endowed progress effect.

In the 1930s, psychologist Clark Hull saw rats run faster the closer they got to food.

In 2006, a study of a café coffee card found the same: customers sped up as the free coffee got closer.

slides.lead: People rarely quit because the road is long.
slides.accent: They quit when it feels like they haven’t started.

slides.line: Save this for the next thing you keep putting off.

caption:
In 2004, a car wash handed out two loyalty cards: one with 8 empty spaces, one with 10 spaces and 2 already stamped. Both needed the same 8 washes for a free one. 34% finished the pre-stamped card, versus 19%.

Psychologists call it the endowed progress effect: a goal that feels already started is easier to finish.

What would you finish faster if it felt already started?
